extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), patent practitioners overseeing non-practitioner staff, law school clinic supervisors, and applicants using USPTO pro bono services
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, regulatory provisions, program eligibility criteria, and procedural rules governing practice before the USPTO, discipline processes, conflicts, signature requirements, patent-agent privilege, and related ethics matters for patent practitioners and clinic programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility requires willingness and ability to participate; no public discipline by the USPTO or another jurisdiction in the past three years (unless based on same conduct as the investigation); and the misconduct at issue must not involve misappropriation of funds or dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; result in or be likely to result in substantial prejudice to a client or other person; constitute a 'serious crime' (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.1); or be part of a pattern of similar misconduct or be of the same nature as misconduct for which practitioner has been disciplined within the past five years, unless the misconduct is minor and related to a chronic health condition or disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program launched 2017; candidate must both be willing/able to participate and meet the listed exclusions. Use of this program is limited where client harm, dishonesty, serious crime, recent discipline, or pattern of similar misconduct exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro bono program participation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Law School Clinic Certification Program: students in a participating law school's clinic may practice before the USPTO under the strict guidance of a law school faculty clinic supervisor with limited recognition for participating students. USPTO Patent Pro Bono Program: regional programs match financially under-resourced inventors/small businesses with volunteer practitioners to file and prosecute patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law school clinic practice requires faculty supervision and certification (see www.uspto.gov/lawschoolclinic). Patent Pro Bono operates via independent regional programs; inventors/attorneys should use www.uspto.gov/probonopatents to find regional links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities constituting practice before the USPTO (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.5(b) & 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office includes communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the office; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the office; consulting with or giving advice regarding filing a trademark application or other non-patent matters (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is broad. Practitioners may employ or retain non-practitioner assistants under the supervision of the practitioner to assist in matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office; supervision obligations still apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance definition and investigation process (37 C.F.R. § 11.1; § 11.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'grievance' is 'a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). Upon receiving a grievance the OED Director may request information and evidence from the grievant, the practitioner, or any person reasonably expected to provide needed information (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations can be initiated by any written submission meeting the definition. Expect document and testimonial requests from the OED Director to those with relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible OED dispositions after investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conclusion of an investigation the OED Director may: close the investigation without issuing a warning or taking disciplinary action; issue a warning to the practitioner; institute formal charges upon approval of the Committee on Discipline; or enter into a settlement agreement with the practitioner and submit it for approval of the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes range from no action to formal charges; settlement agreements require Director approval. Self-reporting is often considered a mitigating factor in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint filing deadlines (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing for filing a complaint: within one year after the date on which the OED Director receives a grievance. No complaint may be filed more than ten years after the date on which the misconduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants and counsel should note both deadlines: 1-year from Director's receipt of grievance and absolute 10-year bar from misconduct date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline and interim suspension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.24, 11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed based on discipline by a state or federal program or agency and is often conducted on the documentary record only (37 C.F.R. § 11.24). Interim suspension may be imposed based on conviction of a serious crime and referred to a hearing officer for determination of final disciplinary action (37 C.F.R. § 11.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline imposed elsewhere can trigger USPTO proceedings without new fact-finding. Criminal convictions can produce immediate interim suspension pending further proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patent-agent privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-agent privilege is recognized only as to those activities that patent agents are authorized to perform (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)). Communications are privileged if 'reasonably necessary and incident to' the ultimate patent prosecution; communications outside that scope (e.g., strategy for product development rather than seeking patent protection) are not covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Queen’s University (Fed. Cir. 2016) recognizes limited privilege; Onyx v. Cipla (D. Del. 2019) refused protection for communications not incident to patent prosecution. Practitioners should restrict privileged communications to agent-authorized activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized Practice of Law (UPL) prohibitions and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not hold themselves out as attorneys when they are not, must avoid dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation, and must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.31(d)(1), 10.89(c)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Campbell (USPTO Apr. 29, 2014) — a patent agent who represented a client in non-patent criminal and civil matters and claimed to be a 'federal attorney' was excluded from USPTO practice. Avoid misrepresenting status or acting outside authorized scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision, disclosure, and conduct that aids UPL (In re Chow example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must supervise non-practitioner staff, disclose referral/payment arrangements to clients, and not permit non-practitioners to draft and communicate with clients without adequate supervision. Aiding UPL and failure to disclose material business relationships are sanctionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Chow: agent's customer number was used for ~6,760 applications with non-practitioners drafting work and undisclosed referral/payment relationships — resulted in three-year suspension. Rule highlights include conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(b)(5) & 11.804(d)), aiding UPL (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.47(a),(c) & 11.505), and conflicts provisions (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.62(a), 10.68(a)(1), 11.107(a)(2), & 11.108(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest and client communication obligations (case guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must obtain informed consent where conflicts exist, act competently, abide by client decisions, be diligent, and communicate sufficiently with clients. Taking direction from a third-party payer without client informed consent and preserving independence of judgment is prohibited (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.104, 11.107, 11.303, 11.504(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Starkweather: voluminous referrals from a marketing company without informed client consent, failing to continue client work, and signing clients' names led to a three-year suspension plus CLE and MPRE. Maintain client communication, obtain informed consent in writing for conflicts, and avoid allowing third parties to direct representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent conflict of interest rule (37 C.F.R. § 11.107)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest: (1) representation of one client will be directly adverse to another; or (2) there is a significant risk the representation will be materially limited by duties to another client, a former client, a third person, or a personal interest. Exceptions allow representation if practitioner reasonably believes competent and diligent representation to each affected client is possible; representation not prohibited by law; not asserting claims by one client against another in the same proceeding; and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When potential conflicts exist, obtain and document written informed consent and ensure independence and competence for each affected client; do not represent directly adverse clients nor those with materially limiting risks absent consent and other conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party compensation and independence of judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f) & § 11.504(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from one other than the client unless: (1) the client gives informed consent; (2) there is no interference with the practitioner's independence of professional judgment or with the client-practitioner relationship; and (3) information relating to representation is protected as required by § 11.106. A practitioner shall not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the practitioner to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment in rendering such legal services (37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain client informed consent and preserve independent professional judgment whenever a third party pays or recommends the practitioner; document protections for confidential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for patent documents (37 C.F.R. § 1.4; MPEP § 502.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence requiring a person's signature must be: (i) an original handwritten signature personally signed in permanent dark ink or equivalent, or (ii) a direct or indirect copy of an original. S-signatures are permitted where the person inserting the signature 'must insert his or her own S-signature' and certifies that the inserted signature is his or her own (37 C.F.R. § 1.4(d)). MPEP clarifies 'original' and states the signer must directly type his or her own S-signature; one person may not type another person's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain originals if copies filed; be aware the Office may require originals for authenticity. Do not allow another person (e.g., secretary) to enter a practitioner's S-signature; the signer must personally insert typed signature characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature and certification requirements for trademark documents (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark correspondence requiring a signature must bear a handwritten signature personally signed in permanent ink or a true copy, or an electronic signature personally entered by the signatory. Electronic signature requires the signer personally enter the adopted signature between two forward slashes in the signature block or use another form specified by the Director (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c)). Presentation of any document constitutes a certification under § 11.18(b); violations may jeopardize application/registration validity and lead to sanctions and disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All documents must be personally signed; another person may not sign or type the electronic signature for a qualified practitioner. Violations of signature/certification rules risk application/registration validity and disciplinary consequences. TMEP provides case citations supporting no third-party entry of electronic signatures (In re Dermahose Inc., In re Cowan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable or gross misconduct standards and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disreputable or gross misconduct (e.g., submitting unprofessional or abusive remarks in office action responses) is sanctionable under 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a). Other relevant provisions include discourteous conduct before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 10.89(c)(5)), conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5)), and certification obligations upon filing (37 C.F.R. § 11.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example In re Schroeder: unprofessional remarks stricken and six-month suspension by default where aggravating factors (no remorse) existed. Practitioners should avoid discourteous or unprofessional communications and comply with filing certifications.
